question.text: $R \Leftrightarrow S \equiv$
question.explanation:
According to the definition of the biconditional,

  • $A \Leftrightarrow B$ is true if $A\Rightarrow B$ and $B\Rightarrow A.$ Otherwise, it is false.

  • In other words, $A \Leftrightarrow B$ is true if $A$ and $B$ have the same truth values. Otherwise, it is false.

So in this case, we have \[ R \Leftrightarrow S \equiv (R \Rightarrow S) \land (S \Rightarrow R). \]

question.text:
\[ X \Leftrightarrow (Y \land X) \equiv \bbox[3pt, white, border: 1pt solid black]{\phantom{AAAAAAAAAA}} \land \big[(Y \land X) \Rightarrow X\big] \]

What expression should be inserted into the blank space above to give logically equivalent statements?
question.explanation:
According to the definition of the biconditional,

  • $A \Leftrightarrow B$ is true if $A\Rightarrow B$ and $B\Rightarrow A.$ Otherwise, it is false.

  • In other words, $A \Leftrightarrow B$ is true if $A$ and $B$ have the same truth values. Otherwise, it is false.

So, in this case, we have

\[ X \Leftrightarrow (Y \land X) \equiv \big[\,\bbox[2pt, Gainsboro]{\color{blue}X \Rightarrow (Y \land X)}\big] \land \big[(Y \land X) \Rightarrow X\big]. \]

Therefore, the missing part is $ X \Rightarrow (Y \land X).$

\[ \lnot P \Leftrightarrow (P \lor Q) \, \equiv \, \big[\lnot P \Rightarrow (P \lor Q)\big] \land \bbox[3pt, white, border: 1pt solid black]{\phantom{AAAAAAAAAA}} \]

What expression should be inserted into the blank space above to give logically equivalent statements?
question.explanation:
According to the definition of the biconditional,

  • $A \Leftrightarrow B$ is true if $A\Rightarrow B$ and $B\Rightarrow A.$ Otherwise, it is false.

  • In other words, $A \Leftrightarrow B$ is true if $A$ and $B$ have the same truth values. Otherwise, it is false.

Therefore, in this case, we have

\[ \lnot P \Leftrightarrow (P \lor Q) \, \equiv \, \big[\lnot P \Rightarrow (P \lor Q)\big] \land \big[\,\bbox[2pt, Gainsboro]{\color{blue}(P\lor Q) \Rightarrow \lnot P}\,\big]. \]

Therefore, the missing part is $(P \lor Q) \Rightarrow \lnot P.$

According to the definition of the biconditional,

  • $A \Leftrightarrow B$ is true if $A\Rightarrow B$ and $B\Rightarrow A.$ Otherwise, it is false.

Therefore, the missing part is $Y \Rightarrow \lnot (Y \land X).$

question.explanation:
According to the definition of the biconditional,

  • $A \Leftrightarrow B$ is true if $A\Rightarrow B$ and $B\Rightarrow A.$ Otherwise, it is false.

  • In other words, $A \Leftrightarrow B$ is true if $A$ and $B$ have the same truth values. Otherwise, it is false.

So in this case, we have \[ P \Leftrightarrow Q \equiv (P \Rightarrow Q) \land (Q \Rightarrow P). \]

question.text: $\lnot (R \Leftrightarrow \neg S)\equiv$
question.explanation:
First, we use the definition of the biconditional statement to write the equivalence as a conjunction of implications: \[ \lnot (R \Leftrightarrow \lnot S) \equiv \lnot \big[(R \Rightarrow \lnot S) \land (\lnot S \Rightarrow R)\big] \]

Now, we represent all the implications using disjunctions and negations: \[ \lnot \big[(R \Rightarrow \lnot S) \land (\lnot S \Rightarrow R)\big] \equiv \lnot \big[(\lnot R \lor \lnot S) \land (\lnot\lnot S \lor R)\big] \]

Next, we simplify the double negations: \[ \lnot \big[(\lnot R \lor \lnot S) \land (\lnot\lnot S \lor R)\big] \equiv \lnot \big[(\lnot R \lor \lnot S) \land (S \lor R)\big] \]

Now, we use De Morgan's laws: \begin{align*} \lnot \big[(\neg R \lor \neg S) \land (S \lor R)\big] &\equiv \lnot (\neg R \lor \lnot S) \lor \lnot (S \lor R) \\[5pt] &\equiv (\lnot\lnot R \land \lnot\lnot S) \lor\lnot (S \lor R) \end{align*}

Finally, we again simplify the double negations and write down symbols in alphabetic order inside the parentheses using commutative laws: \begin{align*} (\lnot\lnot R \land \lnot\lnot S) \lor \lnot (S \lor R) &\equiv (R \land S) \lor \lnot (S \lor R) \\[5pt] &\equiv (R \land S) \lor \lnot (R \lor S) \end{align*}

question.text: $\lnot (R \Leftrightarrow S)\equiv$
question.explanation:
First, we use the definition of the biconditional statement to write the equivalence as a conjunction of implications: \[ \lnot (R \Leftrightarrow S) \equiv \lnot \big((R \Rightarrow S) \land (S \Rightarrow R)\big) \]

Now, we represent all the implications using disjunctions and negations: \[ \lnot \big((R \Rightarrow S) \land (S \Rightarrow R)\big) \equiv \lnot \big((\lnot R \lor S) \land (\lnot S \lor R)\big) \]

Next, we use De Morgan's laws: \begin{align*} \lnot \big( (\lnot R \lor S) \land (\lnot S \lor R)\big) &\equiv \lnot (\lnot R \lor S) \lor \lnot (\lnot S \lor R) \\[3pt] &\equiv (\lnot\lnot R \land \lnot S) \lor (\lnot\lnot S \land \lnot R) \end{align*}

Finally, we simplify the double negations: \begin{align*} (\lnot\lnot R \land \lnot S) \lor (\lnot\lnot S \land \lnot R) &\equiv (R \land \lnot S) \lor (S \land \lnot R) \end{align*}

question.text: $\lnot (Y \Leftrightarrow X)\equiv$
question.explanation:
First, we use the definition of the biconditional statement to write the equivalence as a conjunction of implications: \[ \lnot (Y \Leftrightarrow X) \equiv \lnot \big[(Y \Rightarrow X) \land (X \Rightarrow Y)\big] \]

Now, we represent all the implications using disjunctions and negations: \[ \lnot \big[(Y \Rightarrow X) \land (X \Rightarrow Y)\big] \equiv \lnot \big[(\lnot Y \lor X) \land (\lnot X \lor Y)\big] \]

Next, we use De Morgan's laws:

\begin{align*} \lnot \big[(\lnot Y \lor X) \land (\lnot X \lor Y)\big] &\equiv \lnot (\lnot Y \lor X) \lor \lnot (\lnot X \lor Y) \\[5pt] &\equiv (\lnot\lnot Y \land \lnot X) \lor (\lnot\lnot X \land \lnot Y) \end{align*}

Finally, we simplify the double negations: \begin{align*} (\lnot\lnot Y \land \lnot X) \lor (\lnot\lnot X \land \lnot Y) &\equiv (Y \land \lnot X) \lor (X \land \lnot Y) \end{align*}

question.text: $ \lnot A \Leftrightarrow B \equiv $
question.explanation:
First, we use the definition of the biconditional statement to write the equivalence as a conjunction of implications: \[ \lnot A \Leftrightarrow B \equiv (\lnot A \Rightarrow B) \land (B \Rightarrow \lnot A) \]

Now, we represent all the implications using disjunctions and negations:

\[ (\lnot A \Rightarrow B) \land (B \Rightarrow \lnot A) \equiv ( \lnot \lnot A \lor B) \land ( \lnot B \lor \lnot A) \]

Next, we use De Morgan's laws: \[ (\lnot \lnot A \lor B) \land ( \lnot B \lor \lnot A) \equiv ( \lnot \lnot A \lor B) \land \lnot (B \land A) \]

Finally, we simplify the double negations: \[ (\lnot \lnot A \lor B) \land \lnot (B \land A) \equiv (A \lor B) \land \neg (B \land A) \]

question.text: $\lnot (B \Leftrightarrow A) \equiv$
question.explanation:
First, we use the definition of the biconditional statement to write the equivalence as a conjunction of implications: \[ \lnot (B \Leftrightarrow A) \equiv \lnot \big[(B \Rightarrow A) \land (A \Rightarrow B)\big] \]

Now, we represent all the implications using disjunctions and negations: \[ \lnot \big[(B \Rightarrow A) \land (A \Rightarrow B)\big] \equiv \lnot \big[(\lnot B \lor A) \land (\lnot A \lor B)\big] \]

Next, we use De Morgan's laws: \begin{align*} \lnot \big[(\lnot B \lor A) \land (\lnot A \lor B)\big] &\equiv \lnot (\lnot B \lor A) \lor \lnot (\lnot A \lor B) \\[5pt] &\equiv (\lnot\lnot B \land \lnot A) \lor (\lnot\lnot A \land \lnot B) \end{align*}

Finally, we simplify the double negations and write down symbols in alphabetic order inside the parentheses using commutative laws: \begin{align*} (\lnot\lnot B \land \lnot A) \lor (\lnot\lnot A \land \lnot B) &\equiv (B \land \lnot A) \lor (A \land \lnot B) \\[5pt] &\equiv (\lnot A \land B) \lor (A \land \lnot B) \end{align*}
